impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that patent claims covering humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies for treating headache were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity for Teva's headache patents covering the use of humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies to treat headache. The court found error in the invalidity determination despite the specification disclosing only one specific humanized antibody (G1, the active ingredient in Ajovy). This decision is significant for the pharmaceutical industry as it addresses the scope of patent protection available for antibody-based therapeutics.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens patent holders' ability to obtain and enforce genus claims for antibody-based therapeutics even when the specification discloses a limited number of specific embodiments, supporting broader patent protection for biologic drugs.
impacts.negativeImplications: May make it harder for generic and biosimilar manufacturers to invalidate broad antibody patent claims on written-description or enablement grounds, potentially extending periods of market exclusivity for branded biologics.

impacts.caseName: Trustees of Columbia University v. Gen Digital Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to detecting anomalous program executions by comparing function calls made in an emulator to a model of expected function calls are directed to an abstract idea under Alice step one, and whether the district court erred in awarding damages based on foreign sales.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated a $185 million jury verdict, holding that Columbia's computer security patents claiming methods for detecting anomalous program executions were abstract at Alice step one and required remand for step two analysis. The court also held that the district court erred in awarding damages for foreign sales and vacated enhanced damages and attorneys' fees that relied in part on an improper contempt finding against Norton's counsel.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides defendants with stronger grounds to challenge software and cybersecurity patents under § 101 eligibility. The foreign sales ruling limits patent damages to domestic conduct, protecting companies from extraterritorial patent liability.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the software and cybersecurity space face heightened risk that their claims will be found abstract under Alice, potentially undermining the value of computer security patent portfolios.

impacts.caseName: Global Tubing LLC v. Tenaris Coiled Tubes LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether genuine disputes of material fact precluded summary judgment on inequitable conduct in obtaining patents and on a Walker Process antitrust fraud claim for attempted monopolization.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment on both inequitable conduct (which had been granted against Tenaris) and a Walker Process antitrust fraud claim (which had been granted in favor of Tenaris), finding genuine disputes of material fact on both issues. The case involved Tenaris's acquisition of prior art (CYMAX Documents) and allegations that Tenaris failed to disclose this material prior art during patent prosecution. The decision sends both the patent unenforceability and antitrust claims back for trial.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of inequitable conduct benefit from the court's recognition that factual disputes preclude summary judgment, preserving the right to trial. Patent challengers benefit from the revival of the Walker Process antitrust claim.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders who acquire prior art through corporate acquisitions face significant risk if that prior art is not disclosed during prosecution. The revived Walker Process claim exposes Tenaris to potential antitrust liability for attempted monopolization through enforcement of allegedly fraudulently obtained patents.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether there was a legally sufficient evidentiary basis to support the jury's finding that the asserted trade secrets were protectable under California law, and whether the counterfeiting verdict was supported by sufficient evidence.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the denial of JMOL on trade secret misappropriation claims, finding insufficient evidence that the asserted trade secrets were protectable because the underlying information was generally known. The court also vacated the reasonable royalty, exemplary damages, and permanent injunction related to the trade secret claims. However, the court affirmed the counterfeiting liability and damages for unauthorized use of the Penuma® trademark.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides a strong defense for companies accused of trade secret misappropriation where the allegedly secret information is generally known in the field. Reinforces the requirement that trade secret plaintiffs must prove their information is not generally known.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret holders face a higher evidentiary burden to establish protectability, and jury verdicts finding trade secret misappropriation may be overturned as a matter of law if the information is found to be generally known.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court correctly granted summary judgment of noninfringement based on extraterritoriality and rejection of VLSI's doctrine of equivalents theory for patent claims relating to multi-core processor task allocation.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit addressed Intel's summary judgment of noninfringement of VLSI's '836 patent relating to selecting processor cores based on speed parameters. The court's ruling on the extraterritoriality of patent infringement and the scope of doctrine of equivalents has significant implications for semiconductor and technology companies with global manufacturing and design operations.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies with global operations benefit from clarity on extraterritorial limits of U.S. patent infringement, potentially shielding foreign manufacturing and design activities from U.S. patent liability.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders asserting infringement against companies with distributed global operations face obstacles in capturing the full scope of infringing activity under U.S. patent law.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court correctly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment of patent eligibility for certain claims of the '761 and '700 patents directed to non-uniform constellations in communication systems, while affirming eligibility for claims of the '509 and '922 patents. The court also affirmed the denial of JMOL on non-infringement and damages. This decision is significant for the telecommunications industry and standard-essential patent licensing.
impacts.positiveImplications: Affirming eligibility for some claims and the damages verdict preserves patent holders' ability to enforce communication technology patents and collect substantial royalties from implementers of industry standards.
impacts.negativeImplications: The partial vacatur on eligibility creates uncertainty for holders of patents claiming mathematical or algorithmic improvements to communication systems, and may require retrial on eligibility for affected claims.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative testimony is admissible at summary judgment regardless of personal knowledge, and whether the on-sale bar under 35 U.S.C. § 102(b) requires that prior art sales expressly disclose the device's functionality.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the on-sale bar, holding that Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representatives may testify beyond their personal knowledge at summary judgment and that the on-sale bar does not require that prior art sales expressly disclose the device's functionality. The court also held that computer source code constituting machine commands is not hearsay.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens invalidity challenges by allowing broader use of Rule 30(b)(6) testimony and computer source code as evidence. Companies defending against patent assertions benefit from a more expansive on-sale bar doctrine.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face increased vulnerability to on-sale bar challenges, as competitors can rely on corporate representative testimony from witnesses without personal knowledge of historical sales and on source code evidence to prove prior commercial activity.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC correctly found that Apple's importation and sale of Apple Watch models with blood oxygen measurement functionality violated Section 337 of the Tariff Act by infringing Masimo's patents covering wearable blood oxygen measurement devices.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the ITC's finding that Apple violated Section 337 by importing Apple Watches with blood oxygen functionality that infringed Masimo's patents. The court upheld the Commission's domestic industry determination, validity rulings, and infringement findings, sustaining the limited exclusion order barring importation of infringing Apple Watch models. This high-profile decision significantly impacts the wearable health technology market.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in the wearable health technology space are strengthened in their ability to use ITC proceedings to block importation of infringing consumer electronics products, providing powerful enforcement leverage.
impacts.negativeImplications: Major technology companies integrating health monitoring features into consumer devices face significant risk of import bans through ITC enforcement actions, potentially requiring costly product redesigns or licensing agreements.

impacts.caseName: Actelion Pharmaceuticals Ltd v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' in pharmaceutical composition patents refers to pH measured at a temperature standard in the field, and whether Actelion was barred from asserting infringement under the doctrine of equivalents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding of no literal infringement and no infringement by equivalents of Actelion's epoprostenol formulation patents. The court held that 'a pH of 13 or higher' refers to pH measured at a standard temperature in the field, and that Actelion was barred from asserting its doctrine of equivalents theory. This ruling clears the path for Mylan's generic epoprostenol drug.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic pharmaceutical manufacturers benefit from the ruling, which enables market entry for generic epoprostenol products. The decision provides clarity on pH claim construction in pharmaceutical patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies face narrower patent protection where claim terms reference physical measurements that are temperature-dependent, and may be precluded from relying on doctrine of equivalents if not properly preserved.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an ITC respondent may obtain a mandatory stay under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) of a refiled declaratory judgment action after having missed the statutory deadline for seeking a stay of its original action involving the same parties and issues.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that a respondent in an ITC proceeding cannot circumvent the statutory deadline for a mandatory stay under § 1659(a)(2) by dismissing and refiling the same declaratory judgment action. BioMarin had missed the 30-day deadline for seeking a stay in Ascendis's original DJ action and attempted to obtain a mandatory stay by filing a new DJ action. The ruling prevents gamesmanship with mandatory stay provisions in parallel ITC and district court proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Protects patent holders from strategic manipulation of mandatory stay provisions by ITC respondents, ensuring that parallel district court litigation can proceed when statutory deadlines are missed.
impacts.negativeImplications: ITC respondents who miss the 30-day mandatory stay deadline cannot cure the defect by refiling, limiting their ability to manage parallel litigation strategy.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding the plaintiff's damages expert report for using an improper royalty base and subsequently granting summary judgment based on absence of a remedy.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's exclusion of Exafer's damages expert report and vacated the summary judgment based on absence of a remedy in a patent infringement case involving Microsoft's Azure platform networking technology. The court found that the district court applied too rigid a standard in excluding the expert's opinions and erred in granting summary judgment solely because the damages evidence was excluded.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent plaintiffs benefit from a more permissive standard for damages expert testimony, reducing the risk that technical deficiencies in a damages report will result in case-dispositive exclusion and summary judgment.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies defending patent suits may face greater difficulty in obtaining summary judgment through Daubert motions targeting damages experts, potentially increasing litigation costs and trial exposure.

impacts.caseName: Willis Electric Co., Ltd. v. Polygroup Ltd. (Macao Commercial Offshore)
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly denied Polygroup's JMOL of obviousness and motion for a new trial on damages for a patent covering pre-lit artificial trees with integrated mechanical and electrical connections.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's denial of JMOL of obviousness and new trial on damages, upholding the jury's verdict that Willis's patent on pre-lit artificial trees with simultaneous mechanical and electrical connections was not obvious. The decision sustains patent protection for an innovation widely used in the consumer holiday products market.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in the consumer products space benefit from the affirmance of the validity verdict and damages award, supporting enforcement of patents on practical consumer innovations.
impacts.negativeImplications: Competitors in the pre-lit artificial tree market remain subject to patent infringement liability, potentially limiting product design options and requiring licensing.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Board erred in its obviousness determination of the challenged patent claims, and whether a non-party filing IPR petitions on the same day as the time-bar deadline for a litigation party raises privity or real-party-in-interest concerns under 35 U.S.C. § 315(b).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the Board's obviousness determination for FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent and remanded for further proceedings. The case raised significant concerns about potential circumvention of the IPR one-year time bar, as Qualcomm filed IPR petitions challenging the same patents asserted against Roambee on Roambee's filing deadline despite not being a party to the underlying litigation.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders benefit from the vacatur of the obviousness finding and the court's scrutiny of potential time-bar circumvention through third-party IPR filings, which may deter coordinated petitioning strategies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that rely on third parties to file IPR petitions face increased scrutiny regarding privity and real-party-in-interest relationships, potentially limiting strategic options for challenging patents outside the one-year time bar.

impacts.caseName: National Veterans Legal Services Program v. United States
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly approved the $125 million class action settlement of claims that the federal judiciary overcharged PACER users, and whether incentive awards to nonprofit class representatives were permissible.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed approval of a $125 million nationwide class action settlement resolving claims that the federal judiciary charged excessive PACER fees to fund expenses unrelated to PACER's operation. The court upheld the settlement terms, attorneys' fees, and incentive awards to the three nonprofit class representatives, rejecting all objections raised by a pro se objector. Hundreds of thousands of PACER users will be reimbursed.
impacts.positiveImplications: Affirms the viability of class action settlements involving government fee overcharges and validates incentive awards for nonprofit class representatives, supporting organizational standing in consumer class actions.

impacts.caseName: mCom IP, LLC v. City National Bank of Florida
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly dismissed patent claims as invalid on obviousness grounds at the pleading stage and whether the case qualified as exceptional under 35 U.S.C. § 285 warranting attorneys' fees.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed dismissal of mCom's patent infringement complaint for failure to state a claim, finding the surviving patent claims invalid on the same obviousness grounds that invalidated the other claims in IPR. However, the court reversed the § 285 exceptional case fee award and the § 1927 sanctions against mCom's counsel, finding insufficient grounds to support either determination. This clarifies the standards for fee-shifting in patent cases.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides patent litigants with protection against excessive fee-shifting, clarifying that filing suit on claims that survived IPR, even if ultimately unsuccessful, does not automatically make a case exceptional under § 285.
impacts.negativeImplications: Defendants who successfully invalidate patents at the pleading stage may not recover attorneys' fees absent a strong showing of exceptionality, limiting deterrence against weak patent assertions.
